tools.summary: Of the open-source generators reviewed here, cdxgen covers the most layers. Its `aibom` command and `-t ai` project type catalog models (GGUF, safetensors, ONNX, pickle checkpoints), Hugging Face purls with revisions, inference providers, agent frameworks, instruction and skill files, and MCP configurations, MCP Registry manifests and MCPB bundles . It deliberately emits derived signals (counts, flags, tool names, scopes) rather than raw instruction text, so secrets in rules files do not leak into the BOM (B2-07). Two cautions. Its `cdx:mcp:*`, `cdx:agent:*`, `cdx:tool:*` and `cdx:skill:*` properties sit under the `cdx` namespace, which the CycloneDX taxonomy reserves for registered sub-namespaces . Its MCP pinning flag, experimental and off by default, records whether a server package carries a hash; it does not digest tool definitions . Releases currently ship under two npm names: @cdxgen/cdxgen 13.6.0 (31 Oct 2026) and @cyclonedx/cdxgen 12.9.0 (22 Oct 2026) . CycloneDX 2.0 agent-behavior output is planned in issue #4593, not shipped (B2-06) . cdxgen also records GitHub Actions properties such as SHA pinning and id-token permissions , signs BOMs with JSF through `cdx-sign` , and traces a running process with `tracebom` .

tools.summary: The OWASP AIBOM Generator builds CycloneDX 1.6 AIBOMs for open models on Hugging Face and scores how complete each one is . It lives under the OWASP GenAI Security Project, not the separate OWASP AIBOM Project at owaspaibom.org (A7-03) . Native CycloneDX fields carry what they can (model card parameters, considerations, licenses, supplier); SPDX-AI-style fields such as autonomyType and safetyRiskAssessment go into bare metadata properties, and GGUF and tokenizer details into `genai:aibom:modelcard:*` (B6-05) . It is a build-time complement to runtime inventory and says nothing about agents, tools or instructions.

tools.summary: k8s-aibom is an unprivileged Kubernetes controller that writes a CycloneDX 1.6 ML-BOM for each AI workload it detects: serving runtimes, agent frameworks, vector databases, training jobs and evaluation harnesses . Google open-sourced it on 13 July 2026; the latest release is v1.6.2 (22 Oct 2026) . Its best idea is the confidence model: every attribute is declared, inferred, verified or unresolved, with an evidence locator, and 'verified' requires an OMS/Sigstore signature that matches an operator-configured signer (A7-01). Its limits matter for agents. It does not see MCP servers, tool schemas, skills or prompts, and it does not sign its own BOMs (A7-01); models downloaded at runtime are invisible ; and its README warns that zero matches is never proof of absence (A7-08) . NVIDIA's AI Cluster Runtime adopted it under ADR-019 and notes that signing runtime observations still needs a separate design .

tools.summary: agent-harness-aibom inventories a running Hermes or OpenClaw installation: the harness binary, models behind its endpoint, MCP servers, tools, skills, hooks, prompt surfaces and credential files (locations and permissions only) . It stays inside the CycloneDX 1.6 schema where a native field exists and puts the rest under a `harness-aibom:` namespace, validated in its tests (B6-04) . It is the clearest published example of tool-definition digests in a BOM: once a server is probed, `definitionSha256` covers name, description and inputSchema, and unprobed tools are flagged `mcp_tool_not_pinned` (B6-09) . Probing is opt-in and HTTP-only, and the hash uses sorted-key JSON rather than RFC 8785, so digests are not comparable with other tools. It signs BOMs with cosign keys and gates CI with its policy command.

tools.summary: Invariant Labs released mcp-scan in April 2025 after its tool-poisoning disclosure; version 0.3.0 'detects changes to MCP tools via hashing' to catch rug pulls . Snyk renamed it Snyk Agent Scan, and the PyPI mcp-scan package is now a redirect (A3-04, B6-07) . Version 0.6.10 (30 Oct 2026) discovers MCP servers and skills across agent clients including Claude Code, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Windsurf and Gemini CLI, retrieves tool descriptions and reports scored risks such as prompt injection, destructive capabilities and malicious skills . Three cautions for production use: it starts stdio MCP servers to read their tools, so its README says to scan untrusted configs in a sandbox; analysis sends MCP server configurations, tool names and descriptions, and skill content (secrets redacted) to Snyk's Agent Scan API under a SNYK_TOKEN, which matters if agent configuration may not leave the network; and its JSON output is marked experimental . The current README no longer describes hash-based pinning, so confirm before relying on it for rug-pull detection.

Its type vocabulary is among the largest here, but CycloneDX has no native component types for most of it: the reporter maps agents and MCP servers to `application`, tools to `library` and skills to `file`, and keeps the real type in a `cisco-aibom:type` property (B6-11) . tools.summary: The Model Provenance Kit answers one question: does this model derive from a known base family? It compares eight fingerprints, from architecture metadata and tokenizer to weight statistics, against about 150 base models from 45+ families . It produces similarity statistics for lineage, not per-tensor content digests, and is not built to detect a trojaned layer (B5-05). Use it to check a supplier's lineage claim, and use OMS digests for integrity.

tools.summary: cosign is a common way to sign BOMs outside the BOM format itself. `cosign attest --type cyclonedx` attaches a CycloneDX BOM as an in-toto predicate in a DSSE envelope whose subject is a container image digest, avoiding CycloneDX's rarely implemented JSF signatures; for a BOM that describes no image, such as an agent snapshot, `cosign attest-blob` attests to a file you name instead . For SPDX 3.0.1, which has no in-document signing, pass the custom predicate type `--type https://spdx.dev/Document/v3` , because cosign's built-in `spdx` type labels the predicate as SPDX 2 (A7-09, B1-04) . Every statement `cosign attest` builds is labelled in-toto Statement v0.1, not v1 . It is the mechanism, not the inventory: it proves who signed which bytes, not that the BOM is complete or true.

tools.runtime_observation: Runtime Traces predicate exists; no agent-specific predicate
tools.summary: in-toto supplies the statement format almost everyone else uses . OMS and SymBiote emit in-toto Statement v1 in DSSE envelopes (B5-04) , and SLSA Provenance is defined as an in-toto predicate type ; `cosign attest` also wraps its predicates in DSSE but still labels the statement `https://in-toto.io/Statement/v0.1` . Verifiers therefore have to accept both statement versions. None of the vetted predicates is ML- or agent-specific (B5-14) . A tool-definition-set or agent-snapshot predicate would have to be defined by a profile and, ideally, proposed upstream.

tools.summary: TAIBOM adds a trust layer on top of AI BOMs: identity, dependencies, annotations and inferencing, expressed as W3C verifiable credentials, with transitive risk propagation . It stresses that the T means 'trustable (not trustworthy)' (B6-08) . It has no agent-specific component types. All evidence comes from the project homepage source; the working-docs pages were not reachable and no implementation or license was identified, so the entry is partially verified (B6-08) .

tools.name: Syft

inventories_by_layer.model: GGUF and SafeTensors catalogers (header metadata, including Docker Model Runner OCI layers) in v1.55.0
inventories_by_layer.delivery: Packages across many ecosystems in images, filesystems and archives

tools.output_formats: CycloneDX, SPDX (2.3 default; 3.0 JSON opt-in), Syft JSON and others
tools.signing_attestation: syft attest wraps the SBOM in a signed in-toto attestation by invoking cosign (cosign must be installed)
tools.summary: Syft is a mainstream software SBOM generator; when asked for SPDX it writes 2.3 by default, with 3.0 available only in JSON (B4-09) . With cosign installed, `syft attest` signs its SBOM as an in-toto attestation . Its README lists no AI ecosystem, which the register took as weak evidence of no model support (B7-05). The v1.55.0 source shows otherwise: it ships GGUF and SafeTensors catalogers that read model headers, including Docker Model Runner OCI layers . It still knows nothing about agents, tools or instructions.

tools.name: Microsoft sbom-tool
tools.open_source: yes (MIT); does not accept outside contributions
tools.version_status: Tag v4.1.13 (tracked by Homebrew because the last GitHub release no longer builds)

inventories_by_layer.model: none
inventories_by_layer.delivery: Software packages and files

tools.output_formats: SPDX 2.2 (default); SPDX 3.0 opt-in (-mi SPDX:3.0) writes specVersion '3.0', which strict SPDX 3.0.1 validators reject (inference from code)
tools.summary: sbom-tool generates SPDX 2.2 by default; SPDX 3.0 is opt-in and hard-codes specVersion '3.0', which does not match the 3.0.1 SemVer pattern (B4-07) . Homebrew tracks tag v4.1.13 because the last GitHub release no longer builds . It has no AI or agent coverage.

tools.name: brox
tools.owner: 'brox Contributors' (repository links are an unfilled placeholder)

inventories_by_layer.model: LLM endpoints and agent frameworks
inventories_by_layer.tools: MCP servers and their capabilities as brox.capability.record strings with scope and evidence
inventories_by_layer.identity: Egress domains; capability scopes such as filesystem.write
inventories_by_layer.delivery: PR capability diff

tools.output_formats: 'CycloneDX-compatible' JSON, specVersion 1.5; README sample uses component type 'service', which fails schema validation
tools.summary: brox is real, though thin: one PyPI release, 0.1.0 (13 Feb 2026), that turns agent, tool and model changes into a pull-request capability diff (B6-01) . Its repository links point to a template placeholder, and its README sample declares CycloneDX 1.5 but gives an MCP server the component type 'service', which no CycloneDX schema from 1.5 to 1.7 allows (B6-01) . With a single release, placeholder links and a schema-invalid sample, brox reads as an early prototype of a pull-request capability diff rather than a production tool.

tools.name: Official MCP Registry
tools.version_status: Preview since 2025-09-08; v0.1 API freeze since 2025-10-24; latest dated server.json schema 2025-12-11; repository tag v1.8.7 (2026-10-30)

inventories_by_layer.model: none
inventories_by_layer.tools: Server metadata (packages, remotes, repository, version); no tool definitions
inventories_by_layer.identity: Namespace ownership via GitHub OAuth/OIDC or DNS/HTTP challenges
inventories_by_layer.delivery: Immutable version metadata; fileSha256 required only for MCPB bundles and not validated by the registry

tools.output_formats: server.json (JSON Schema); REST API v0.1
tools.signing_attestation: No attestation, signature or provenance field in server.json
tools.summary: The official MCP Registry launched in preview on 8 Sep 2025 and froze its v0.1 API on 24 Oct 2025 . It verifies namespace ownership , and published version metadata cannot be changed . It does not verify that a publisher controls a remote server's URL, does not itself validate the hash it requires for MCPB bundles (MCP clients check it at install time), and tells consumers to 'assume minimal-to-no moderation' . server.json has no attestation, signature or provenance field and no tool definitions (B6-03) . Treat a registry entry as a pointer, not as evidence.

tools.name: agent-bom
tools.open_source: yes (Apache-2.0, per PyPI license_expression; repository github.com/koda-ai-studio/agent-bom)

inventories_by_layer.model: AI packages
inventories_by_layer.tools: MCP clients, servers, tools, transports, trust posture
inventories_by_layer.runtime: MCP proxy/gateway with inline firewall enforcement (claimed in PyPI description; not inspected)
inventories_by_layer.identity: Summary says it maps 'what each one can reach' (not inspected)
inventories_by_layer.delivery: AI packages

tools.output_formats: CycloneDX and SPDX (versions not checked), SARIF, OCSF and others
tools.runtime_observation: MCP proxy/gateway claimed in PyPI description; not inspected
tools.summary: agent-bom (koda-ai-studio) scans MCP clients, servers and tools plus rules and skill files (B6-11). It outputs CycloneDX, SPDX, SARIF and OCSF, and its description claims an MCP proxy/gateway with inline firewall enforcement . It reports coverage, warning that 'incomplete evidence is not clean'. It releases very often (177 releases since February 2026). Only its PyPI description was reviewed, so it is partially verified and its runtime and enforcement claims are untested.

tools.name: Trusera ai-bom

inventories_by_layer.model: LLM and API integrations, agent frameworks
inventories_by_layer.tools: MCP server configurations; n8n AI nodes
inventories_by_layer.runtime: Separate trusera-sdk intercepts HTTP calls and evaluates Cedar policies
inventories_by_layer.delivery: none

tools.output_formats: CycloneDX 1.6, SPDX 3.0, SARIF, JSON

tools.name: mcplock

inventories_by_layer.model: none
inventories_by_layer.tools: Lockfile of MCP tool definitions with four hashes: content (description + inputSchema), description, schema, annotations
inventories_by_layer.runtime: Diff against the lockfile when run
inventories_by_layer.delivery: none

tools.output_formats: Lockfile; CI exit codes
tools.summary: mcplock is 'npm audit / SRI for MCP tools': it pins each tool with separate content, description, schema and annotations hashes, so a flipped destructiveHint shows up as its own finding, and it treats a missing baseline as a failure (B6-09) . It is a CI lockfile tool, not a BOM.

tools.name: mcp-pin

inventories_by_layer.model: none
inventories_by_layer.delivery: none

tools.output_formats: unknown
tools.signing_attestation: Seals its hash-chained guard log via --sign-command (ssh-keygen -Y sign, smartcard or KMS CLI); the .mcp-pin.lock approval baseline is unsigned
tools.runtime_observation: Compares on use; guard, gateway and a PreToolUse hook refuse tool calls whose digest drifted from the lockfile
tools.summary: mcp-pin is a zero-dependency 'approve once, refuse what changed' pin for MCP servers and skills . Its own README states the limit every pinning tool shares: pinning detects change, not initial honesty, so a tool poisoned from its first approved version passes (B6-02). Its guard log can be sealed with an external signing command, but the lockfile itself is unsigned: the README notes that guard 'cannot tell your lock from someone else's'.

tools.name: aibom-scanner

inventories_by_layer.model: AI SDK usage in code
inventories_by_layer.tools: Flags MCP servers launched without a pinned package version
inventories_by_layer.delivery: Maps findings to NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001, EU AI Act and OWASP lists

tools.output_formats: Table, JSON, SARIF (not CycloneDX)
tools.summary: aibom-scanner matters for one idea: every scan reports what it actually read (coverage_pct, incomplete_inputs), and `--fail-on-incomplete-coverage` fails the build when it could not parse something. 'An AI Bill of Materials that silently omits what it could not parse is not incomplete, it is wrong' (B6-09) . Its output is not a CycloneDX BOM.

tools.name: picklescan

inventories_by_layer.model: Blocklist scan of pickle files for dangerous callables
inventories_by_layer.delivery: Model intake

tools.output_formats: Console report; exit codes
tools.summary: picklescan is an open-source blocklist scanner for pickle files; the Hugging Face Hub runs a similar import scan on every uploaded pickle and highlights suspicious imports . picklescan has had 59 security advisories (58 CVEs) against v0.0.20, almost all detection bypasses, fixed between v0.0.21 (Feb 2025) and v1.0.4 (Mar 2026) . Use it for triage; the robust control is not to load untrusted pickles at all (see fickling below).

tools.name: fickling

inventories_by_layer.model: Static analysis of pickles; allowlist hook for ML imports at load time
inventories_by_layer.delivery: Model intake

tools.output_formats: Analysis reports
tools.summary: fickling's `activate_safe_ml_environment()` checks pickle imports against an allowlist of ML-library imports and blocks everything else, which is sturdier than a blocklist scan but is not a sandbox (lens controls-06) . fickling itself has fixed 16 security advisories between 0.1.6 and 0.1.12 . The robust control is not to load pickles from untrusted sources at all: prefer safetensors, which does not execute code on load , or `torch.load(weights_only=True)` , and keep scanners for triage.

evidence_urls: SymBiote specification v0.1 (collectors.md, attestation.md, digests.md); repository private
tools.summary: SymBiote is the author's AgentBOM toolkit and is listed for comparison, with its status taken from the specification and the SymBiote document's implementation table, not from an independent test; its row is a self-assessment. AgentBOM is the name of SymBiote's profile; it is unrelated to the agent-bom tool from koda-ai-studio reviewed above. It computes a typed SHA-256 digest (tooldef/v1) over the RFC 8785 canonical JSON of each tool's model-visible fields, taken from the raw `tools/list` JSON-RPC result, exports CycloneDX 1.7 and SPDX 3.0.1 that validate against the official schemas, signs snapshots as in-toto statements with Sigstore or keys, and exports a Gateway Allowlist Bundle that a reference check enforces (SymBiote spec: digests.md, attestation.md, collectors.md). The specification defines 14 collectors. MCP configuration and ShadowScan import run from the CLI; live `tools/list`, OpenTelemetry traces, MCP registry resolution and k8s-aibom import exist as Python APIs not yet wired into the CLI; a hosted-models module exists, but the README still lists hosted models as in progress; instructions, skills, frameworks, local models, Agent Cards, identity configuration and SBOM merge are in progress. Approvals are not yet keyed by authorization context, and the trust-status signing CLI is in progress, which is why G1 and G9 are rated P. It is alpha software in a private repository.
